analysis.one_liner: Requires doctors who treat Medicare patients to accept Medicare's approved payment as full payment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare at the time, doctors could 'not accept assignment,' meaning they could bill Medicare patients an extra amount on top of Medicare's approved fee, leaving seniors to pay the difference. This bill would have required Medicare payments for physician services to be made only 'on assignment' — doctors would have to accept Medicare's approved charge as payment in full, with no extra billing of the patient. It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would no longer pay doctors' excess charges above Medicare's approved fee for physician services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries facing extra doctor bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Medicare part B to provide that payment for physicians' services 'only [be made] on an assignment-related basis,' effective October 1, 1989.

Assignment-based payment means the doctor accepts Medicare's approved charge as payment in full, eliminating patient responsibility for the balance, a cost shift that falls on seniors living on fixed incomes.

analysis.who_pays: Physicians, who would lose the ability to collect excess charges above Medicare's approved fee from Medicare patients.

drawbacks.text: Doctors could respond to lower Medicare fees by limiting the Medicare patients they accept, which could reduce seniors' access to care — a trade-off Congress had recently confronted when a mandatory-assignment provision in the 1988 Medicare catastrophic care law was repealed in 1989 after strong physician opposition.
Capping what doctors can collect from Medicare patients reduces physician revenue without adding new Medicare funding, leaving the pressure on doctors' practices rather than on government budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a direct, tangible saving to Medicare beneficiaries by banning extra billing, at the cost of physician income and a possible risk that some doctors would see fewer Medicare patients. The core trade-off — patient savings versus physician pay — is real, and the legitimate concern that payment caps can affect access to care is the strongest objection. It was a blunt instrument, but it targeted a cost seniors bear directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, forwarded to their health subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Donnelly introduced the bill on January 3, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce.
On February 6, 1989, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and on January 11, 1989, to a Ways and Means health subcommittee.
No markup, vote, or floor action followed, and the bill died in committee when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians benefited from the bill's death because they kept the ability to bill Medicare patients above Medicare's approved fee. Seniors gained nothing; the extra charges the bill would have eliminated remained legal.

for.name: Rep. Brian J. Donnelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Medicare physician payments be made on an assigned basis.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Medicare part B
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 1989, and referred it to a health subcommittee; never reported the bill or scheduled action on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 1989, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; never took further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and drew no recorded votes, so no partisan split was ever measured; its subject matter, limiting what doctors can charge Medicare patients, put it at odds with organized medicine rather than with a party bloc.

industries.note: The bill would have required doctors to accept Medicare's approved fee as payment in full, eliminating the excess charges they can collect from Medicare patients. Physicians' ability to bill seniors above the Medicare rate is exactly what the bill would end, so the industry's interest in the bill ran against patients' pocketbooks.
